'Dhibali' is their own name. Speakers are called 'Babali'. SVO.. 2 causatives; aspect; comparatives; 3 tones; stress; 9 vowels." followed by 'Riverine. Tropical forest. 500 meters. Swidden agriculturalists.' which the report rightly omits. The 16th edn. file has the same line as '.. comparatives; tonal, 3 tones; stress; 9 vowels.' and the Google Books s…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule is given: Ethnologue records only that Bali is a three-tone language that also has stress. No opened source says where the stress falls. The only first-hand-derived phonological remarks found (Grégoire 2003, p. 357, drawing on Bolingola 1995) say the language has three tones (high, mid, low) and that its tone system is 'not sufficiently known yet'; they say nothing about stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Database typology string; no domain stated (word vs phrase), no examples, no locus. It asserts only that Bali has three tones and stress.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources refer to the same language: Bali/Kibali/Libaali/Dhibali of Bafwasende Territory (Tshopo), Guthrie D21, ISO bcp = bali1274. Ethnologue names four dialects (Bemili, Bakundumu, Bafwandaka, Bekeni; Bemili central); Richardson 1957 likewise distinguishes four dialects by sector. Grégoire 2003 p. 357 writes 'Bira (D21)', which by the Guthrie code is Bali (Bira is D32); the three-tone remark is therefore taken as referring to Bali. Not to be confused with Bali/Mungaka (Cameroon), Bali-Vitu, or Baali/Wiinza-Baali (Ngombe C40) in Motingea's work.

On Bali (D21): eight vowels, incipient nasalized vowels, phonological vowel length, labiovelars (pp. 351-353); p. 357: 'some northernmost languages of zone D and C have three tones: high, mid and low.
